newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Support for Sweden's ruling party rises - polls.
newsitem.headline: Support for Sweden's ruling party rises - polls.

text.p: Sweden's ruling Social Democrats were continuing to gain support in the country's opinion polls due to signs the economy was improving after the party slumped to a six year low in popularity earlier this year.

Two polls published on Friday showed the minority Social Democrats kept their position as Sweden's most popular party for the second consecutive month in June after falling behind the opposition conservatives, the Moderates, earlier in 1997.
A survey by pollster SKOP found the Social Democrats support rose to 38.6 percent in June from 35.8 percent in May and 31.5 percent in April.
The Moderates continued a downward slide, despite the return of popular leader, Carl Bildt, who has come back to domestic politics after over two years as an international peace mediator in Bosnia.
The Moderates' support fell to 26.8 percent in June from 29.2 percent in May and 31.9 percent in April.

SKOP said support for the Social Democrats, led by Prime Minister Goran Persson, was now back to the same levels as June last year although this was still seven percentage points below its 45.3 percent ranking in the 1994 general election.
The Moderates won 22.4 percent of the vote in 1994.
The pollster attributed the better numbers to growing optimism among Swedes that the economy was finally improving after three hard years with cuts and restructuring.
"Economic optimism is returning and many Swedes expect better times after the economic reorganisation," analyst Birgitta Hultaker said in a statement.
But she said continuing high unemployment in Sweden, running at 7.8 percent in May, remained a threat to the Social Democrats in the run-up to the next general election in September 1998.

A Temo poll, published by daily newspaper Dagens Nyheter, showed the Social Democrats with 33.5 percent of support in June against 27 percent in February and the Moderates with 32.5 percent compared with 31.5 percent.
The pollster said both Persson and Bildt needed the support of other parties in the seven-party parliament to secure next year's election.

The Left Party won 10.5 percent of support in the June poll (9.0 percent May), the Greens 7.0 percent (9.0 percent), the Centre party 6.5 percent (5.0 percent), the Liberal 5.0 percent (6.5 percent) and the Christian Democrats 3.5 percent (4.0 percent).
